entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Hillel ben Samuel (died 1295) was a pivotal Italian Jewish intellectual of the 13th century, renowned as a physician, philosopher, and Talmudist whose work bridged the intellectual currents of the Latin West and the Arabic-Hebrew philosophical traditions. Operating from Verona and later Ferrara, his contributions were critical in transmitting and interpreting the complex Aristotelian and Maimonidean thought to a broader European Jewish audience, thereby shaping the intellectual landscape of medieval Judaism. His intellectual lineage was distinguished, being the grandson of Eliezer ben Samuel of Verona, a prominent Tosafist.

His primary philosophical undertaking was the translation and commentary of significant Arabic philosophical texts into Hebrew, most notably the 'Treatise on the Intellect' by Averroes (Ibn Rushd). Hillel's original work, *Tagmule ha-Nefesh* (Recompense of the Soul), completed around 1290, meticulously explores the nature of the soul, divine providence, and human free will, often engaging directly with the doctrines of Maimonides and Averroes. As a physician, he studied at Salerno, a leading medical school, and served various patrons, applying his scientific acumen to practical healing while integrating philosophical and ethical considerations into his medical practice. His intellectual endeavors were not confined to philosophy; he also engaged in halakhic discussions, demonstrating a comprehensive grasp of Jewish law and tradition.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hillel ben Samuel played a crucial role in the transmission of Greco-Arabic philosophy to Jewish scholars in Europe through his translations and original works. His efforts significantly shaped the intellectual discourse on faith and reason within medieval Jewish thought, impacting subsequent generations of philosophers.
